analysis.one_liner: Extends federal equal-pay protection to cover sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, and sex stereotypes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 7 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act, the law behind the federal Equal Pay Act, to make clear that "sex" includes sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics such as intersex traits, sex stereotypes, and pregnancy or childbirth. That would let workers who are paid less because of who they are bring the same federal equal-pay claims that women have long been able to bring. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are paid less because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, intersex traits, or because they are pregnant or stereotyped about their sex. Under the Equal Pay Act these workers currently have weaker or unclear federal protection against being paid less than coworkers doing the same work; the bill would have put them squarely under the same protection [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics including intersex traits, sex stereotypes, and pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions to the definition of 'sex' in the Fair Labor Standards Act, so all of these count in federal equal-pay claims [S2] [S3].
Changes the equal-pay provision's wording from 'opposite sex' to 'another sex,' covering workers whose employer points to a nonbinary or nonmatching comparison to dodge a claim [S2] [S3].

This matters because the federal Equal Pay Act, which lives inside the Fair Labor Standards Act, lets workers recover back pay when they are paid less than a coworker of a different sex for the same work; the bill would extend that tool to workers the current text does not clearly name.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who are paying workers of different sexual orientations, gender identities, or pregnancy statuses unequal wages for the same work would have to make up the difference, plus potential back pay. Employers generally would face new compliance obligations in reviewing pay structures [S3].

drawbacks.text: Employers would bear the cost of auditing and equalizing pay structures and could face back-pay claims from workers previously paid less, a real compliance cost even for employers acting in good faith [S3].

Critics argue the change is partly unnecessary: the Supreme Court's Bostock decision already read 'sex' in Title VII to include sexual orientation and gender identity, so opponents could claim courts were moving in this direction without new legislation — though that ruling applies to Title VII, not directly to the Equal Pay Act provision this bill amends.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: workers who today have weak or unclear federal protection against being underpaid for who they are would gain the same equal-pay remedy other workers have. The cost falls on employers who must equalize pay, which is the point of the law — workers in those cases gain what their employers lose. The main design question is whether courts were already converging on this reading, but codifying it removes uncertainty rather than adding burden beyond equal pay itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2021, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Anthony G. Brown of Maryland introduced the bill on November 30, 2021, with six Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind: the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and bills that die at the end of a Congress must be reintroduced from scratch in the next one.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay workers unequally because of sexual orientation, gender identity, or pregnancy keep the status quo, where those workers have weaker federal equal-pay claims. No one else's situation changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping the unequal-pay status quo

for.name: Rep. Anthony G. Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor

for.name: Reps. Higgins (NY), Kildee, Maloney (NY), Moulton, Roybal-Allard, and Tonko
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced; no other cosponsors ever joined

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor (Chair Bobby Scott)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's last recorded action is the referral itself

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the partisan shape can only be inferred: all 7 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored [S4].

industries.industry: Employers generally (businesses covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed any employer paying workers less based on sexual orientation, gender identity, intersex traits, or pregnancy to equal-pay claims and back-pay liability. Its interest in avoiding that liability runs against the workers the bill protects.
